sections.title: Glaciers built by hand
sections.intro_md:
In **October 2013**, an engineer and school reformer named **Sonam Wangchuk** ran a pipe from a stream above Leh down to the valley floor and let the water spray into the freezing night air. By spring it stood about **6 metres** tall and held roughly **150,000 litres** of water, enough to irrigate fields in April and May.

He called it an **ice stupa**, after the Buddhist reliquary mounds that dot every village.

That is Ladakh in one idea. A place where it rains about **100 mm a year**, less than parts of the Sahara, where every barley field depends on meltwater, and where people have spent a thousand years engineering around scarcity. It is also a place now arguing loudly about who gets to decide its future, and the man with the pipe is at the centre of that argument too.

spotlights.name: The ice stupa
spotlights.spot_it: A tall white cone of ice standing alone in a brown valley in March, often with prayer flags strung from its tip.
spotlights.story_md: A cone is the trick. For the volume of water it holds, it shows very little surface to the sun, so it melts slowly and late. Water is piped from a stream higher up the valley and pushed out of a vertical pipe by its own pressure; in temperatures far below zero, it freezes as it falls. The first prototype in **2013** held about **150,000 litres**. Since **2019** villages have competed in an annual **Ice Stupa Competition**, and Wangchuk won a **Rolex Award for Enterprise in 2016** for the idea. The design has since been copied in Switzerland, Chile and Kyrgyzstan.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned winter water, which usually runs to waste, into spring irrigation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Freeze the winter, drink it in spring.

spotlights.name: Chewang Norphel's artificial glaciers

where.label: Phuktse and villages of the Leh district

spotlights.spot_it: Long, shallow terraces of ice on a shaded hillside, held back by low stone walls, far below any natural glacier.
spotlights.story_md: Before the ice stupa there was **Chewang Norphel**, a civil engineer born in **1935**, nicknamed the **Ice Man of Ladakh**. He noticed that water trickling slowly under poplar trees froze, while fast water nearby did not. So he diverted streams onto shaded slopes and slowed them with stone check-walls, building sheets of ice at low altitude that melt **earlier** than the real glaciers, just when spring sowing needs water. Accounts credit him with **12 to 15** such glaciers. He received the **Padma Shri in 2015**. Wangchuk's ice stupa was partly an answer to the problem of Norphel's design: flat ice on low ground melts too fast once the sun climbs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that villages could store water as ice, with nothing but stones and gradients.
spotlights.memory_hook: Slow the water, and the cold does the rest.

sections.title: Ladakh at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh is India's **largest union territory** and its **emptiest**. The area India administers is about **59,146 km²**, bigger than Himachal Pradesh, yet the 2011 census counted only **274,289 people**, about **4.6 per km²**.

It sits between the Great Himalaya and the Karakoram, mostly above **3,000 metres**. Leh, the main town, is at about **3,500 m**.

Until **31 October 2019** it was part of the state of Jammu and Kashmir. Since then it has been a union territory **without a legislature**, run by a Lieutenant Governor, with two elected **Hill Councils** in Leh and Kargil. In 2011 Muslims (mainly Shia) were about **46%** of the people and Buddhists about **40%**, with Hindus at 12%. Leh district is mostly Buddhist; Kargil district mostly Muslim.

spotlights.name: Leh
spotlights.spot_it: A flat-roofed mud-brick town in a dry bowl of mountains, with a nine-storey palace and a red gompa on the ridge above it.
spotlights.story_md: Leh grew because it sat on the caravan road between **Kashmir, Tibet and Yarkand** in Central Asia. Traders brought pashmina wool, salt, tea, silk, horses and Chinese silver through its bazaar, and the main street is still wide because it was built for caravans. At about **3,500 m**, it is one of the highest towns in India, and visitors who fly in are told to rest for **48 hours** before doing anything. Its air is so thin that flights land and leave in the early morning, before the afternoon winds rise. Leh district had about **133,000** people in 2011.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where nearly every visitor, trader and soldier entering Ladakh has passed through.
spotlights.memory_hook: A caravan town that still has caravan-wide streets.

spotlights.name: Khardung La
spotlights.spot_it: A crowded summit sign covered in stickers and prayer flags, with army trucks and motorbikes parked in snow.
spotlights.story_md: Signboards at the top proudly claim **5,602 m** and 'the world's highest motorable road'. Satellite data and GPS surveys put the pass at about **5,359 m**, which is still very high, but not the record the sign claims. It is the gateway from Leh to the **Nubra valley** and on to the Siachen glacier. Long before cars, it was on the caravan route to **Kashgar and Yarkand**, and about **10,000 horses and camels** a year are said to have crossed it. The Border Roads Organisation built the motor road in **1976**; a tunnel is planned below it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Ladakh's most famous road and a lesson in checking numbers on signs.
spotlights.memory_hook: The sign says 5,602. The satellites say 5,359.

sections.title: A cold desert on the roof of India
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh is a **high-altitude cold desert**. The Himalaya to the south blocks the monsoon, so the valleys get rain-shadow skies: intense sun by day, frost by night, and winter lows of **minus 20 to minus 30°C**.

Four great ranges run across it from northwest to southeast: the **Great Himalaya**, the **Zanskar range**, the **Ladakh range** and the **Karakoram**. Between them run the rivers. The **Indus** enters from Tibet near Demchok and flows past Leh. The **Zanskar** joins it at Nimmu.

To the east lies **Changthang**, an extension of the Tibetan plateau at 4,000 to 5,000 m, with salt lakes such as **Pangong Tso**, **Tso Moriri** and **Tso Kar**. In the north, the Nubra valley has something nobody expects at this height: sand dunes and two-humped camels.

spotlights.name: Pangong Tso
spotlights.spot_it: A long, narrow lake that changes from turquoise to deep blue as the light moves, set between bare ochre mountains.
spotlights.story_md: Pangong Tso is about **134 km long** but only about 5 km wide at most. Roughly **two-thirds** of it lies in territory held by China, and the **Line of Actual Control** runs through the water. Its western part is salty and it has no outlet, yet it **freezes solid** in winter. The final scene of the 2009 film **3 Idiots** was shot on its shore, and tourist numbers exploded afterwards. In **2020** the north bank's mountain spurs, known as the 'fingers', became a flashpoint between Indian and Chinese troops. A buffer zone was agreed in February 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Ladakh's most photographed place and a live border.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lake two countries share and one film made famous.

spotlights.name: Tso Moriri
spotlights.spot_it: A wide, still blue lake ringed by snow peaks, with a few white houses of Korzok village on its western shore.
spotlights.story_md: Tso Moriri lies at about **4,522 m**, higher than Pangong, and is less visited because it is a long, rough drive from Leh. It was named a **Ramsar wetland of international importance in 2002**. It is one of the few breeding grounds in India of the **black-necked crane** and the bar-headed goose, a bird that migrates over the Himalaya. The only permanent village on its shore, **Korzok**, is home to Changpa herders and a small gompa, and is among the highest permanently inhabited villages in the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the quieter, wilder twin of Pangong, protected for its birds.
spotlights.memory_hook: Higher, colder, quieter: the lake the cranes chose.

spotlights.name: Hunder dunes, Nubra valley
spotlights.when: Old caravan stage on the road to Yarkand
spotlights.spot_it: Grey sand dunes between snow peaks, with a line of shaggy two-humped camels and green sea buckthorn scrub along a river.
spotlights.story_md: The **Nubra valley**, across Khardung La from Leh, is where the Shyok and Nubra rivers meet. At about **3,100 m**, it is lower and warmer than Leh, and the river has heaped up white-grey sand dunes around **Hunder**. On them graze India's only herd of **Bactrian camels**, descended from animals that carried goods on the Silk Road caravans to Yarkand until the route closed around **1950**. Today they carry tourists for short rides. The army also trialled them as pack animals for high border posts in the 2020s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living leftover of the Silk Road inside India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sand dunes and two-humped camels at 3,000 metres.

spotlights.name: Chadar, the frozen river road
spotlights.spot_it: A line of walkers in bright jackets shuffling on a sheet of white ice at the bottom of a deep, narrow canyon.
spotlights.story_md: In deep winter the **Zanskar river** freezes along its gorge and becomes a road, the *chadar*, or blanket. For centuries it was the only way in or out of **Zanskar** once the passes were snowed shut. Families walked it to reach Leh, monks carried supplies, and children came home from school on it. The route is about **105 km**, the gorge walls rise up to 600 m and narrow to about 5 m in places, and night temperatures fall to **minus 30°C** and below. Now it is also a famous trek. A new road along the gorge will make the winter walk unnecessary for locals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how winter isolation shaped Zanskar's life.
spotlights.memory_hook: In January the river turns into a road.

spotlights.name: The Indus and Zanskar confluence
spotlights.spot_it: Two rivers meeting in a gorge: one blue-green, the other muddy brown, flowing side by side before they mix.
spotlights.story_md: Just below **Nimmu**, about 35 km from Leh, the **Zanskar** joins the **Indus**. In summer the colours differ sharply: the Indus usually runs clear blue-green and the Zanskar silty brown, and they flow side by side before they blend. This is the river that gave **India its name**: the Sanskrit *Sindhu* became the Persian *Hindu* and the Greek *Indos*. In India, the Indus flows only through **Ladakh** and a short stretch beyond, which is why its banks at Shey host a national **Sindhu Darshan** festival every June.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's namesake river runs through Ladakh.
spotlights.memory_hook: Blue meets brown at the river that named India.

sections.title: Life at four thousand metres
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh's animals are built for thin air, cold and scarce food.

The top predator is the **snow leopard**, the UT's official animal since **2021**. Its prey includes **blue sheep (bharal)**, **Asiatic ibex** and the rare **Ladakh urial**. On the open Changthang plateau live **kiang**, the Tibetan wild ass, and a few **Tibetan gazelles**; wolves follow the herds. The UT bird is the **black-necked crane**, which nests in Changthang's marshes.

**Hemis National Park**, south of Leh, is one of the best places in the world to see snow leopards, and winter tours, when the cats come down to lower valleys, have become a small industry. The flip side is conflict: snow leopards and wolves raid livestock pens, and villages have built predator-proof corrals and homestay schemes so that a living leopard is worth more than a dead one.

spotlights.name: Snow leopard
spotlights.spot_it: A pale grey cat with dark rosettes, a very long thick tail and pale eyes, almost invisible against rock.
spotlights.story_md: India's first scientific count, released on **30 January 2024**, estimated **718 snow leopards** in the country. **Ladakh had about 477** of them, roughly two-thirds. The cat cannot roar. It uses its tail, almost as long as its body, as a balance pole on cliffs and as a scarf when it sleeps. In **Hemis National Park** density reaches about two cats per 100 km², among the highest anywhere. Winter guides in villages such as **Rumbak** and **Ulley** track them for visiting photographers, and families earn more from homestays than from their herds.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ladakh is the snow leopard's stronghold in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The grey ghost: two-thirds of India's snow leopards live in Ladakh.

spotlights.name: Kiang, the Tibetan wild ass
spotlights.spot_it: A large chestnut-and-white wild ass, bigger than a donkey, standing in small herds on open grassland near lakes.
spotlights.story_md: The **kiang** is the largest wild ass in the world, up to about **1.4 m** at the shoulder. In Ladakh it lives on the **Changthang** plateau, around Tso Kar, Tso Moriri and Hanle. Herds can gallop alongside jeeps at speed. Herders sometimes resent them, because a herd grazes the same thin pastures that their pashmina goats need, and the conflict has grown as livestock numbers rose. Kiang are protected under India's Wildlife Protection Act.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the big grazer of Ladakh's high plateau.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wild donkey the size of a horse, racing jeeps.

spotlights.name: Black-necked crane

where.label: Changthang marshes, Hanle and Tso Kar

spotlights.spot_it: A tall grey crane with a black neck and head and a small red crown, wading in pairs in high marshes.
spotlights.story_md: The **black-necked crane** is the only crane that breeds on high plateaus, and Ladakh's **Changthang** is its only breeding ground in India. Only a few dozen birds breed here, with a few pairs nesting each summer in marshes near Hanle, Tso Kar and Tso Moriri, so every nest is counted. It winters in lower parts of Tibet, Bhutan and Arunachal Pradesh. In Buddhist culture across the Himalaya it is a sacred bird, and Ladakhi songs praise it. Free-ranging dogs, which eat eggs and chicks, are its biggest local threat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Ladakh's rarest and most cherished bird.
spotlights.memory_hook: A few pairs, every nest counted, every year.

spotlights.name: Bactrian camel
spotlights.spot_it: A shaggy brown camel with two humps, much woollier than the one-humped camels of Rajasthan.
spotlights.story_md: The two-humped **Bactrian camel** belongs to the cold deserts of Central Asia. Caravans on the Leh to **Yarkand** route used them until trade stopped around 1950, when the borders closed after China took control of Xinjiang and Tibet. Some animals were left behind in Nubra, and their descendants, a population of a **few hundred**, are India's only Bactrian camels. In the 2020s the army trialled them for carrying loads of up to **170 kg** to high posts, where mules struggle. Tourist rides at Hunder keep the herd fed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the last living link to the Silk Road trade through Ladakh.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two humps, two hundred years of caravans, one valley left.

sections.title: Rock carvings, giant Buddhas and the first temples
sections.intro_md:
People have been in Ladakh for thousands of years. Hunters and herders carved **ibex, yaks, hunters and horses** into boulders along the Indus, especially around **Domkhar**, **Tangtse** and the lower Indus valley.

Buddhism came early, from **Kashmir**, perhaps in the Kushan period around the first centuries CE. Ladakh then became a crossroads: Kashmiri art and Indian Buddhism came up the valleys from the south and west, Tibetan language and culture from the east after about the **10th century**.

The key figure of that second wave is the translator **Rinchen Zangpo** (958 to 1055), sent from western Tibet to Kashmir to bring back texts and artists. Alchi, the most famous, may in fact be later, but its paintings preserve something that has almost vanished: the style of Kashmir's Buddhist painters before Kashmir became Muslim.

spotlights.name: Rock art of the Indus valley
spotlights.spot_it: Pecked outlines of ibex with huge curved horns on dark, sun-varnished boulders by the road.
spotlights.story_md: Along the Indus and in places such as **Domkhar** and **Tangtse**, thousands of figures have been pecked into boulders whose surfaces have turned dark with 'desert varnish'. The **ibex**, with its swept-back horns, is by far the commonest subject; some scholars read it as a symbol of fertility and water. Others show hunters with bows, horses with riders, masks and later Buddhist stupas. Many sites have no fence, and road widening and graffiti have damaged several. Researchers have been documenting them since the 1980s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the oldest record of people in Ladakh.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ladakh's first artists drew ibex on rocks.

spotlights.name: The Mulbekh Maitreya
spotlights.when: Probably 7th to 8th century; some claim earlier
spotlights.spot_it: A tall standing Buddha carved in shallow relief on a single rock face, half-enclosed by a small temple building.
spotlights.story_md: Beside the Srinagar to Leh highway at **Mulbekh** stands a figure of **Maitreya**, the Buddha of the future, about **9 metres** tall, carved into a rock pillar. Its style, with a tall crown and slim body, points to Kashmiri sculptors, and most scholars date it to around the **7th or 8th century**, though local tradition places it in the Kushan era. It stands in **Kargil district**, now mostly Muslim, a reminder that Buddhism once ran further west. The road bends around it, and lorry drivers stop to light butter lamps.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It marks the old western edge of Buddhist Ladakh.
spotlights.memory_hook: The future Buddha has been watching the highway for 1,200 years.

spotlights.name: Alchi
spotlights.spot_it: Low mud-walled temples by the Indus whose dark interiors are covered floor to ceiling in fine, many-coloured paintings.
spotlights.story_md: Alchi is not a working monastery but a cluster of small temples whose worship stopped in about the **15th century**, which helped protect their art. Tradition credits **Rinchen Zangpo**; inscriptions suggest the main halls were built around **1150 to 1225** by local patrons. The **Sumtsek**, a three-storey temple, holds clay Bodhisattvas about **4.6 m** tall, whose painted robes show tiny scenes of palaces, pilgrims and court life. A mural of a royal drinking party, with figures in Persian-style robes, is one of the oldest secular paintings in the region. Photography inside is banned to protect the pigments.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It holds the best surviving Kashmiri Buddhist painting anywhere.
spotlights.memory_hook: The lost art of Buddhist Kashmir survives in a Ladakhi village.

sections.title: The Namgyal kingdom
sections.intro_md:
For about **375 years** Ladakh was an independent Buddhist kingdom, ruled from 1460 by the **Namgyal** dynasty.

The kingdom peaked under **Sengge Namgyal**, the 'lion king', in the early 1600s. His family patronised the **Drukpa** school of Buddhism, the same school that ruled Bhutan, and that link nearly destroyed the kingdom.

In **1679**, when Ladakh sided with Bhutan in a quarrel, Tibet and its Mongol allies invaded. Ladakh's king held out in the fort at **Basgo** for three years and then begged help from the **Mughal** governor of Kashmir. Mughal troops drove the invaders back in 1683, at a price: tribute, and a mosque in Leh. The **Treaty of Tingmosgang** (1684) set a border near Demchok that India still cites in its disputes with China.

In **1834** the kingdom fell to **Zorawar Singh**, a general of the Dogra ruler of Jammu. The royal family moved to **Stok**, where it still lives.

spotlights.name: Leh Palace
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, tapering mud-brick palace with small wooden windows, rising nine storeys from the rock above Leh's old town.
spotlights.story_md: The palace was built around **1600** under **Sengge Namgyal**. Its **nine storeys** of stone, mud brick and timber held stables and stores at the bottom and royal rooms at the top. It is often compared to the **Potala** in Lhasa, which it predates: the Potala was begun in **1645**. After the Dogra conquest in the 1830s the family left for Stok, and the palace decayed for more than a century. The **Archaeological Survey of India** has been restoring it since the early 2000s. From its roof you see the whole Indus valley and the Stok range.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the symbol of Ladakh's lost kingdom.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine storeys of mud, built before the Potala.

spotlights.name: Basgo
spotlights.when: Fort and temples 15th to 17th century; siege 1679 to 1683
spotlights.spot_it: Crumbling mud-brick ramparts along an eroded ridge, with a small red-and-white temple perched on top.
spotlights.story_md: Before Leh, **Basgo** was a royal seat, and its fort on a ridge of crumbling clay is where King **Delek Namgyal** held out against the Tibetan and Mongol army from **1679** for about **three years**. The siege only ended when Mughal troops from Kashmir arrived in **1683**. Inside the surviving temples are a large clay **Maitreya** and wall paintings of the 16th century. The site was on the World Monuments Fund watch list in 2000 and was restored with local labour and traditional mud techniques. Erosion still eats the ridge after every rare heavy rain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where the kingdom nearly ended.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three years under siege on a ridge of mud.

spotlights.name: Stok Palace
spotlights.when: Built 1820s; royal home from the Dogra conquest
spotlights.spot_it: A four-storey whitewashed palace with dark window frames on a small hill across the Indus from Leh.
spotlights.story_md: When the Dogras took power, the Namgyal family kept their titles and some lands but lost their throne, and moved across the Indus to **Stok**. The palace, built in the **1820s**, is still their home; part of it is a museum and part a heritage hotel. The museum holds the **royal crown**, a turquoise-covered **perak** headdress, thangkas several centuries old, and swords. The family still plays a ceremonial role at festivals, and members of it have been elected to public office since independence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where the dynasty survived its fall.
spotlights.memory_hook: The kings lost their kingdom and moved across the river.

spotlights.name: Zorawar Singh
spotlights.spot_it: A 19th-century Dogra general, shown in paintings and statues with a turban, sword and moustache.
spotlights.story_md: **Zorawar Singh**, a general of **Gulab Singh** of Jammu, marched into Ladakh in **1834** through the Suru valley with about **5,000 men** and won in a series of campaigns over the next few years. He then took **Baltistan** and, in 1841, invaded **western Tibet**, reaching Taklakot near Lake Manasarovar. Winter caught his army at over 4,500 m. He was killed at the **Battle of To-yo** on **12 December 1841**, and most of his soldiers died of cold. The Treaty of Chushul in 1842 restored the old border. India's army remembers him as a pioneer of high-altitude warfare.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His conquest tied Ladakh to Jammu, and so to India.
spotlights.memory_hook: He took Ladakh in summer and lost Tibet to winter.

sections.title: A frontier of three armies
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh is the only part of India that borders both **China** and **Pakistan**, and since 1947 it has been fought over again and again. The 1947 to 1948 war left Pakistan holding Gilgit and Baltistan and India holding Leh, Kargil and Nubra. In the **1962** war China confirmed its hold on **Aksai Chin**, a high desert India still claims.

The soldiers changed Ladakh as much as the wars did. The army is the region's biggest employer, builder and customer. Thousands of Ladakhis serve in the **Ladakh Scouts**, a regiment known as the 'snow warriors'.

Three flashpoints matter most. The **Siachen glacier**, occupied by India in 1984, is the highest battlefield on Earth. **Kargil**, in 1999, was a short, deadly war on the mountaintops above the Srinagar to Leh road. **Galwan**, in 2020, was the first deadly clash with China in 45 years, fought without guns. After four years of talks, India said in December 2024 that disengagement in eastern Ladakh had been achieved in full.

spotlights.name: Siachen glacier
spotlights.spot_it: A vast river of ice between dark Karakoram peaks, with tiny army huts and helipads on the ridges.
spotlights.story_md: On **13 April 1984**, in **Operation Meghdoot**, Indian troops flown in by helicopter took the heights of the 76 km **Siachen glacier**, days ahead of a Pakistani force. Both armies have stayed since, with Indian posts on the Saltoro ridge at up to about **6,000 m**. Far more soldiers have died from avalanches, frostbite and altitude sickness than from enemy fire. Every drop of fuel and every meal comes by helicopter or on foot. A ceasefire has held since **2003**, but neither side has left. The glacier is also a major source of the Nubra river.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the highest and coldest battlefield in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Here the weather kills more soldiers than bullets.

spotlights.name: The Kargil War

where.label: Tiger Hill and Tololing, Dras sector

spotlights.spot_it: Steep snow-streaked peaks above the Srinagar to Leh highway near Drass, and a pink sandstone war memorial below them.
spotlights.story_md: In spring **1999**, Pakistani soldiers and militants crossed the Line of Control and occupied empty winter posts on the peaks above **Kargil and Drass**, from where they could shell the only road to Leh. India's army fought them uphill, often at night, on slopes above **5,000 m**, while the air force bombed their positions. **Tiger Hill** was retaken on **4 July**, and India declared victory on **26 July**, now **Kargil Vijay Diwas**. India's official toll was **527** soldiers killed. Captain **Vikram Batra**, killed on Point 4875, became a national hero.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first war between two nuclear-armed neighbours.
spotlights.memory_hook: A war fought uphill to save one road.

spotlights.name: The Galwan clash
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow river valley of grey scree and rushing water, at about 4,300 m, near the Line of Actual Control.
spotlights.story_md: On the night of **15 June 2020**, Indian and Chinese soldiers fought in the **Galwan valley** for hours in near darkness. Under old agreements, neither side carried guns at the front, so they fought with **stones, batons and clubs**, some wrapped in barbed wire. **Twenty Indian soldiers** died, including their commander, Colonel **B. Santosh Babu**; several fell into the freezing river. China admitted **four** dead; independent estimates are higher. It was the first deadly clash between the two armies since **1975**, and it triggered four years of standoff along the whole Ladakh border.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reset India's relations with China.
spotlights.memory_hook: No bullets fired, twenty Indians dead.

sections.title: Who lives here, and what they speak
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh's 274,000 people fall into a few main groups. In the Indus valley and Zanskar live **Ladakhi Buddhists**, close in language and culture to Tibet. In **Kargil** and the Suru valley live **Purigpa** and **Balti** people, Shia Muslims who speak Tibetic languages written in Perso-Arabic script. Around **Drass** live **Shina** speakers. In a handful of lower Indus villages live the **Brokpa**, whose language, Brokskat, is related to Shina, not Tibetan. On the eastern plateau live the **Changpa**, nomadic herders.

The 2011 census counted mother tongues like this: **Ladakhi (Bhoti) 40.4%**, **Purgi 33.6%**, Hindi 8.9%, Shina 5.1%, Balti 3.6%, Tibetan 2.3%. In **June 2025** a new regulation made **English, Hindi, Urdu, Bhoti and Purgi** Ladakh's official languages, and promised support for Shina, Brokskat, Balti and Ladakhi.

Ladakhi greet with one word for everything: **Julley**, hello, goodbye and thank you.

spotlights.name: The Changpa nomads
spotlights.spot_it: Black yak-hair tents on a bare plateau, with large flocks of goats and sheep and herders in maroon woollen robes.
spotlights.story_md: The **Changpa** herd yaks, sheep and **pashmina goats** on the Changthang plateau at **4,000 to 5,000 m**, moving camp several times a year along fixed routes. Their traditional tent, the **rebo**, is woven from yak hair, and the gaps let smoke out but keep snow off. Their goats grow the fine underwool that becomes **pashmina** shawls in Kashmir, yet herders get a small share of the final price. Many young Changpa now leave for Leh, and several camps have become settled villages near schools and roads. Hanle's astronomers count some Changpa among their trained star guides.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They produce the raw wool behind the world's most famous shawls.
spotlights.memory_hook: The shawl's story starts in a yak-hair tent.

spotlights.name: The Brokpa of Dha and Hanu

where.label: Dha, Hanu and Garkon, lower Indus

spotlights.when: Villages in the lower Indus valley
spotlights.spot_it: Women and men in hats piled with fresh flowers, silver coins and ribbons, often with long braided hair and heavy jewellery.
spotlights.story_md: The **Brokpa** are a community of about **4,000** in a few villages including **Dha, Hanu, Garkon and Darchik**, in an apricot-rich stretch of the lower Indus. Their language, **Brokskat**, is a form of Shina, from the Dardic group, not Tibetan. They wear tall caps decorated with flowers, keep many old customs around goats and purity, and celebrate a harvest festival called **Bono-na**. Since the 1990s, sensational articles have called them 'the last pure Aryans' and spun stories about foreign women visiting to conceive. Those claims have no scientific basis and are resented by many Brokpa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are a living reminder of the Dardic peoples of the western Himalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: Flowers on the hat, Shina on the tongue.

sections.title: Gompas on the ridges, imambaras in the valleys
sections.intro_md:
Most of Ladakh's Buddhists follow forms of **Tibetan Buddhism**, and its monasteries, called **gompas**, sit on ridges above the villages they serve. Each belongs to a school: the **Gelug** (the Dalai Lama's school) runs Thiksey, Spituk, Likir and Diskit; the **Drukpa Kagyu** runs Hemis, Chemrey and Stakna; the **Drikung Kagyu** runs Lamayuru and Phyang.

The **Dalai Lama** has visited Ladakh often, and since 2017 has spent long summer stays at his residence near Choglamsar, drawing tens of thousands to his teachings.

Kargil district is the other half of the story. Islam came from **Baltistan** and Kashmir from the 15th and 16th centuries, and most Muslims in Kargil are **Shia**, with Muharram processions, black flags and large **imambaras**. Relations are usually close, but they have been strained at times, most sharply in the late 1980s.

rows.Thiksey: Stacked up a hill above the Indus

spotlights.name: Hemis
spotlights.when: Founded in the 1630s under royal patronage
spotlights.spot_it: A large monastery tucked into a side valley, around a wide paved courtyard with painted wooden balconies.
spotlights.story_md: **Hemis** is the richest and best-known monastery in Ladakh, the main seat of the **Drukpa Kagyu** school. It was founded or refounded in the **17th century** under King Sengge Namgyal, whose family were its patrons, and its hidden position in a side valley helped it escape invaders. It holds a huge collection of thangkas, statues and a copper-gilt image of the Buddha. Its courtyard is the stage for the **Hemis Tsechu** masked dances each summer. It is also the setting of a famous 19th-century hoax about Jesus in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the spiritual and financial heavyweight of Buddhist Ladakh.
spotlights.memory_hook: The richest gompa hides in a side valley.

spotlights.name: Thiksey
spotlights.spot_it: Tiers of white monks' houses stacked up a hill to a red-and-ochre temple at the top, like a small Potala.
spotlights.story_md: **Thiksey**, a **Gelug** monastery founded in the 15th century, climbs a whole hill in about **twelve storeys** of buildings and is often compared with Lhasa's Potala Palace. It is home to around 100 monks and a school for young novices. Its **Maitreya** temple holds a seated figure of the future Buddha about **15 m** high, covering two storeys, made of clay and gilded, and installed to mark the **Dalai Lama's** visit in **1970**. Visitors come at dawn for the morning puja, when monks blow long horns from the roof and serve butter tea in the hall.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most photographed gompa in Ladakh.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hill of white houses with a two-storey Buddha inside.

spotlights.name: Lamayuru and Moonland

where.label: Lamayuru, on the Srinagar to Leh road

spotlights.spot_it: A white monastery on a crag above eroded yellow badlands that look like a crumbling sandcastle landscape.
spotlights.story_md: **Lamayuru** is one of Ladakh's oldest monastic sites, now run by the **Drikung Kagyu**. Legend says the valley was once a lake, and the Indian sage **Naropa** made it drain away so a monastery could be built. Geology tells a similar tale: the strange pale formations around the village, nicknamed **Moonland**, are soft sediments laid down in an ancient lake and then carved by wind and water. Lamayuru hosts masked dances called **Yuru Kabgyat** and is a stop on the old road from Kargil to Leh.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the oldest Buddhist sites in Ladakh, on a dried lakebed.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sage drained the lake; the mud became Moonland.

spotlights.name: Diskit and its giant Maitreya
spotlights.spot_it: A huge, brightly painted seated Buddha on a hill, facing down the Shyok river, with an old monastery on the ridge behind.
spotlights.story_md: **Diskit**, founded in the 14th century, is the oldest and largest monastery in **Nubra** and belongs to the Gelug school. Below it sits a seated **Maitreya** about **32 m (106 ft)** tall, consecrated by the **Dalai Lama** in **2010**. It faces down the Shyok valley toward Pakistan, and monks say it is there to protect the village and to pray for peace between the two countries. Inside the old monastery, a much-told local legend claims a mummified hand and head of a demon are kept in a shrine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the landmark of the Nubra valley.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 32-metre Buddha looks toward the border.

spotlights.name: Kargil and its Shia heartland
spotlights.spot_it: A river town of concrete buildings and green poplars on the Suru, with black Muharram banners and domed imambaras.
spotlights.story_md: **Kargil**, Ladakh's second town, sits where the **Suru** and **Drass** rivers meet, halfway between Srinagar and Leh. Most of its people are **Shia Muslims**, and religious life centres on its imambaras and on the learned families who run schools linked to Najaf and Qom. During **Muharram**, processions mourn the death of Imam Husain at Karbala in 680 CE. Before 1947 Kargil was a trading stop toward **Skardu** in Baltistan, now in Pakistan, and families were split by the line. Kargil got its own Hill Council in **2003**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that Ladakh is as much Muslim as Buddhist.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half of Ladakh prays toward Karbala.

sections.title: Masks, archery and a new year that comes early
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh's calendar runs on the Tibetan lunar year, so festival dates move each year.

The heart of most monastery festivals is **cham**, a masked dance performed by monks in silk robes and huge painted masks of protector deities, skeletons, stags and yaks, to the sound of long horns, drums and cymbals. The dances act out the victory of the teachings over evil, and often end with the destruction of an effigy that holds the year's misfortune.

Villages have their own festivals: **archery contests** in spring and summer with music, chang and dancing; harvest festivals; and the winter **Losar**. Since **1997** the government has held **Sindhu Darshan**, a festival on the Indus bank at Shey, to celebrate the river as a national symbol.

data.name: Sindhu Darshan; Hemis Tsechu (June or July)
Phyang Tsedup; Dalai Lama teachings (some years)

spotlights.name: Hemis Tsechu
spotlights.when: 10th day of the 5th Tibetan month, June or July
spotlights.spot_it: Monks in brocade robes and large painted masks whirling slowly in a courtyard, with long horns and cymbals playing.
spotlights.story_md: **Tsechu** marks the birthday of **Padmasambhava** (Guru Rinpoche), the Indian master credited with bringing tantric Buddhism to Tibet. For two days, monks in masks dance in the Hemis courtyard while thousands watch from balconies and roofs. Once every **twelve years**, in the Tibetan **Monkey year**, the monastery unrolls a giant thangka of Padmasambhava several storeys high, embroidered with pearls and precious stones; the last showing was in **2016**, the next due in **2028**. Smaller festivals with the same dances run at Phyang, Thiksey, Lamayuru and Leh Palace.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best-known festival in Ladakh.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every twelve years the monastery unrolls a saint.

spotlights.name: Ladakhi Losar
spotlights.spot_it: Torches carried through dark village lanes at night, flour-dough figures on altars and families in their best woollen robes.
spotlights.story_md: Ladakhi Buddhists celebrate **Losar**, the new year, about **two months earlier** than Tibetans do, in the 11th month of the Tibetan calendar. The usual explanation is a 17th-century king who brought the new year forward so his army could celebrate before going to war in winter. Families clean their houses, make figures of ibex from dough, visit relatives for days and light fire torches called *metho* that are carried through the village to drive out bad spirits. In Leh the festival ends with dancing and singing that can run for a week.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the biggest family festival of the Buddhist year.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ladakh starts its new year two months before Tibet.

spotlights.name: Sindhu Darshan

where.label: Shey Manla, on the Indus near Leh

spotlights.spot_it: Rows of white tents and pilgrims in Indian state dress offering water and prayers on the stony bank of the Indus.
spotlights.story_md: **Sindhu Darshan** began in **1997** as a festival to honour the Indus as a symbol of India's unity, backed by the then BJP leader **L. K. Advani**. Each June, pilgrims from across India bring water from their home rivers in clay pots and pour it into the Indus at **Shey**, then take Indus water home. There are prayers led by priests from different faiths, cultural shows and visits to nearby sites. The festival has made the Indus a stop on India's patriotic map, though many Ladakhis see it as a visitors' event more than their own.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties India's name to Ladakh's river in a yearly ritual.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bring your river, take the Indus home.

sections.title: Turquoise, wool and painted cloth
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh's crafts grew from scarcity. With little wood and no cotton, people wove **sheep and yak wool**, built in mud and stone, carved willow and poplar, and traded for metal, coral and turquoise.

The richest objects are religious: **thangkas** (painted scroll images), clay and gilt statues, painted wooden altars, and the copper and brass of butter lamps and teapots, much of it hammered in the village of **Chilling** on the Zanskar, whose metalworkers are said to descend from Nepali craftsmen brought by a king in the 17th century.

The most valuable thing a Ladakhi family owned was often worn, not displayed: the **perak**, a turquoise headdress handed down through women. Wool was the other wealth.

And everywhere, outside the house, are the crafts of devotion: **prayer flags**, **mani walls** of carved stones and **prayer wheels** turned by hand or by streams.

spotlights.name: Perak, the turquoise headdress
spotlights.when: Heirloom worn at festivals and weddings
spotlights.spot_it: A long leather strip covered in rows of turquoise stones, running from a woman's forehead down her back, with black wool 'ears' on each side.
spotlights.story_md: The **perak** is a band of leather or cloth shaped like a cobra's hood and back, sewn with dozens and sometimes hundreds of **turquoises**, plus coral and silver. It sits on the head and hangs down the back, with flaps of black lambswool over the ears. The number of turquoise rows signalled a family's wealth, and a perak traditionally passed from **mother to eldest daughter**. Women wear it at weddings, festivals and to welcome important guests. Good old peraks are now very valuable, and families keep them locked away much of the year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a bank account worn on the head.
spotlights.memory_hook: The cobra of turquoise passes from mother to daughter.

spotlights.name: Pashmina and the Changthangi goat
spotlights.spot_it: A small white or brown goat with twisted horns and a thick coat, and a featherweight shawl that can be pulled through a ring.
spotlights.story_md: The **Changthangi** goat lives at 4,000 m and more, where winter nights fall below minus 20°C. To survive, it grows an ultra-fine underfleece, the raw material of **pashmina**. Fibres are very fine, about 12 to 15 microns, far finer than a human hair. Each spring herders comb it out by hand, and each goat gives only a few hundred grams. For centuries the wool went by caravan to **Kashmir**, where it was spun and woven into shawls. Ladakh supplies most of India's raw pashmina; India's first cloned pashmina goat, **Noori**, was born in **2012**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Ladakh's most valuable export, though most of the profit is made elsewhere.
spotlights.memory_hook: The shawl that fits through a ring began as a goat's winter vest.

spotlights.name: Thangka painting
spotlights.spot_it: A painted cotton scroll of a deity or mandala, in bright mineral colours inside a frame of silk brocade.
spotlights.story_md: A **thangka** is a Buddhist painting on cotton or silk, mounted on brocade so it can be rolled up and carried, a design suited to nomads and monks on the move. Painters follow strict grids for the proportions of every deity, laid down in old manuals, and grind mineral pigments such as **malachite, lapis and cinnabar**. The work is slow: a detailed thangka can take months. Ladakh's monasteries hold some painted centuries ago, while the giant appliqué thangka at **Hemis** is unrolled only once every twelve years. Young painters now train at Leh's schools and sell to visitors.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how Buddhist teaching is carried in pictures.
spotlights.memory_hook: A painting that rolls up and travels.

spotlights.name: Prayer flags and mani walls
spotlights.spot_it: Strings of blue, white, red, green and yellow cloth squares on passes and roofs, and long low walls of carved stones by the road.
spotlights.story_md: **Prayer flags** come in five colours in a fixed order: **blue** for sky, **white** for air, **red** for fire, **green** for water and **yellow** for earth. Each is printed with prayers and often with the *lungta*, a wind horse carrying a jewel. The idea is that the wind carries the blessings across the land. **Mani walls** are long stone walls covered in flat stones carved with the mantra **Om mani padme hum**. Custom says you should always walk past them **clockwise**, keeping them on your right, and many drivers pass on the left side of the road to obey.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They mark the landscape as Buddhist country.
spotlights.memory_hook: Let the wind do the praying.

sections.title: Barley, butter and apricots
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh's food is built from what grows at 3,000 m and above in a short summer: **barley**, wheat, peas, turnips, potatoes, and apricots in the lower valleys. Meat is mostly mutton and yak, eaten more in winter. Dairy is central: butter, yoghurt, dried cheese called **churpe** and butter tea.

The staple is **tsampa** (*ngamphe* in Ladakhi), roasted barley flour that needs no further cooking. Mixed with butter tea into a dough, it is breakfast in most traditional homes and travel food for herders.

Cooking is slow and warming: soups with hand-made noodles, steamed dumplings called **momos**, and flatbreads called **khambir**.

The lower Indus and Kargil grow some of the world's highest apricots, and trade in dried apricots and kernels, along with **sea buckthorn**, a wild orange berry, has grown fast. Ladakh's white **Raktsey Karpo** apricot got a Geographical Indication tag in **2022**.

spotlights.name: Gur gur cha, butter tea
spotlights.spot_it: A pale, pinkish-beige tea poured from a tall wooden churn or thermos, with a film of butter on top, served salty.
spotlights.story_md: **Gur gur cha** is named for the gurgling sound of the churn. Brick tea is boiled for a long time, then churned with **salt and butter**, sometimes with a little milk or baking soda, in a tall wooden cylinder called a *dongmo*. Hosts keep topping up your cup; to signal you have had enough, you leave it full. Butter tea supplies fat and salt that help in cold, dry air. Sweet milk tea, *cha ngarmo*, is now as common in towns. In a traditional kitchen, the rows of shiny copper and brass pots on shelves were a family's display of wealth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the drink of hospitality and survival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Salty, buttery, never empty: leave your cup full to stop.

spotlights.name: Skyu and thukpa
spotlights.spot_it: A bowl of thick, cloudy stew with pieces of thumb-pressed dough, turnip and potato, or a clear soup with long noodles.
spotlights.story_md: **Skyu** is Ladakh's own pasta: small rounds of wheat dough pressed with the thumb into little cups and boiled with vegetables, root crops and sometimes meat, into a thick stew. **Chhutagi** is its cousin, with dough shaped like bow ties or ears. **Thukpa**, the noodle soup found across the Tibetan world, is lighter and spicier. These dishes are made in one pot over a stove fed with dried dung or wood, which is precious in a land with few trees. Hotels serve them now, but home versions are richer, thickened with flour and butter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are what Ladakh actually eats on a cold night.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pasta pressed by the thumb, cooked in one pot.

spotlights.name: Raktsey Karpo apricots
spotlights.when: Harvest July and August; GI tag 2022
spotlights.spot_it: Orchards of small, pale golden fruit, and rooftops covered with apricots drying in the sun.
spotlights.story_md: Apricot trees grow in Ladakh's lower and warmer valleys, especially in Kargil district, Turtuk and the lower Indus. The famous **Raktsey Karpo** variety has a **white stone**, rare among apricots, and very sweet flesh, and it received a **Geographical Indication** tag in **2022**. Most of the crop has traditionally been sun-dried on roofs, and the kernels are pressed for oil or eaten like almonds. In bloom, in April, the orchards turn white and pink, and spring blossom festivals now draw visitors. Fresh apricots have begun to be flown to markets outside Ladakh.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Ladakh's signature fruit and a growing source of income.
spotlights.memory_hook: An apricot with a white heart.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Traditional Ladakhi life was designed around a short growing season and a long, frozen winter. Families farmed barley in summer, stored fodder, dung and dried vegetables on the roof, and moved the animals into the ground floor in winter, where their warmth helped heat the house.

The British-Swedish writer **Helena Norberg-Hodge** described this world in her book **Ancient Futures** (1991) after years of living in Ladakh from 1975. She argued that its village life had been ecologically balanced and socially secure, and was being undone fast by tourism, development and cash. Critics say she romanticised a hard life with high infant mortality, but the book made Ladakh a global case study.

Some old customs have faded. **Fraternal polyandry**, where brothers shared one wife so that land was not split, was once common in Buddhist families and has disappeared. Yet community labour, called *bes*, still builds houses and cleans irrigation canals, and villages still share water by turn.

And winter has a new sport. **Ice hockey**, played on frozen ponds, is now Ladakh's favourite game.

spotlights.name: The Ladakhi house and dry toilet
spotlights.spot_it: A whitewashed two- or three-storey house with thick sloping walls, small black-framed windows and a flat roof piled with firewood and fodder.
spotlights.story_md: A traditional house is built of **sun-dried mud bricks** on a stone base, with walls thick enough to hold the day's heat into the night. The flat roof, made of poplar beams, willow sticks and packed mud, works because it almost never rains, and it doubles as a store and drying floor. The ground floor is for animals. Upstairs is the **kitchen**, the warmest room, and a family chapel. The **compost toilet**, or *chhagra*, needs no water at all: users add soil after each use, and the waste becomes fertiliser for the fields a year later. Flush toilets in guesthouses have since added to Leh's water stress.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a model of building for climate and scarcity.
spotlights.memory_hook: A toilet that needs no water and feeds the fields.

spotlights.name: Ice hockey on frozen ponds

where.label: Gupuk pond and the NDS rink, Leh

spotlights.spot_it: Players in mixed kit and helmets on a natural ice rink below brown mountains, with crowds standing round in down jackets.
spotlights.story_md: **Ice hockey** is Ladakh's most popular sport, played on natural ice from about mid-December to mid-February, when ponds and flooded fields freeze. Ladakhis have played it since at least the 1970s, often with second-hand kit and on ice they flood and smooth themselves. Leh's teams dominate India's national championships, and the **Ladakh women's team** has represented India abroad. The first **Khelo India Winter Games** were held in Ladakh and Gulmarg in **2020**. An indoor rink in Leh with artificial ice is meant to lengthen the season as winters warm.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how winter itself became a resource.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's ice hockey capital freezes its own rink.

spotlights.name: Ladakhi polo
spotlights.spot_it: Riders on small, sturdy hill ponies swinging long sticks at full gallop on a dusty ground, with a drum and flute band playing.
spotlights.story_md: Ladakh plays a fast, rough, old form of **polo** that came over the mountains from **Baltistan**, where the game has been played for centuries. Teams ride small hill ponies, rules are loose, and a band of **surna** (shawm) and **daman** drums plays faster as the play heats up. **Drass** is the stronghold, with a polo festival each summer, and the Leh polo ground below the palace has hosted matches since royal times. It is one of the few things Ladakhi Buddhists and Muslims celebrate in exactly the same way.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a shared sport across Ladakh's two halves.
spotlights.memory_hook: A drum band that speeds up with the game.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh is small enough that a few people shape its story out of all proportion. Its kings, from **Sengge Namgyal** to the family at Stok, still matter in public memory. And in the 21st century, one engineer became the face of its climate and political fears.

Three stand out. **Kushok Bakula Rinpoche** pulled Ladakh into Indian politics after 1947. **Chewang Rinchen** won India's second-highest military award as a teenager. **Sonam Wangchuk** turned a school reform movement into a global climate campaign and then into a fight for self-rule.

spotlights.name: Sonam Wangchuk
spotlights.spot_it: A slim man with short grey hair, glasses and a round Ladakhi woollen cap, often speaking outdoors in front of a crowd or a glacier.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **1966** in a village without a school, **Sonam Wangchuk** trained as an engineer and in **1988** co-founded **SECMOL**, which reformed Ladakh's failing schools and built a solar-heated campus. His story inspired **Phunsukh Wangdu** in the film **3 Idiots** (2009). He invented the **ice stupa** in 2013 and won the **Ramon Magsaysay Award** in **2018**. He then led the campaign for Sixth Schedule protection and statehood, with fasts and a march to Delhi in 2024. After protests turned violent in September 2025 he was jailed under the **National Security Act** for nearly six months, until **14 March 2026**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the best-known Ladakhi alive and the face of its political protest.
spotlights.memory_hook: The real Phunsukh Wangdu went to jail for Ladakh.

spotlights.name: Kushok Bakula Rinpoche
spotlights.spot_it: A bald monk in maroon robes and glasses, often photographed with Nehru-era politicians or at Leh airport, which bears his name.
spotlights.story_md: Recognised as the reincarnation of an arhat, a disciple of the Buddha, **Bakula Rinpoche** was born into the royal family of Matho in **1917**. After 1947 he led Ladakh's Buddhists into Indian politics, insisting that Ladakh stay with India. He served in the Jammu and Kashmir government and as a Member of Parliament, and was later India's **ambassador to Mongolia** from **1990 to 2000**, where he helped revive Buddhism after communism. Leh's airport is named **Kushok Bakula Rimpochee Airport** in his memory.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made Ladakh's case in New Delhi for half a century.
spotlights.memory_hook: A reincarnated lama became India's man in Mongolia.

spotlights.name: Colonel Chewang Rinchen
spotlights.spot_it: A soldier in uniform with medals, known in Ladakh as the Lion of Ladakh.
spotlights.story_md: **Chewang Rinchen** was only about **17** when he led a militia of local volunteers in **Nubra** in **1948**, holding off raiders and winning the **Maha Vir Chakra**, India's second-highest wartime gallantry award; he remains one of its youngest recipients. In **1971**, as a major, he led the capture of **Turtuk** and nearby villages from Pakistan, and won a second Maha Vir Chakra, one of very few soldiers to win it twice. He is called the **Lion of Ladakh**, and he helped make the Ladakh Scouts a respected fighting force.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is Ladakh's greatest war hero.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two Maha Vir Chakras, the first at seventeen.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors arrive by air at Leh between June and September and do a loop: **Leh** and its gompas, **Nubra** over Khardung La, **Pangong** and back. The roads from **Manali** (about 430 km over four high passes) and **Srinagar** (about 420 km over Zoji La) open roughly from May or June to October or November.

The rest of Ladakh is far less visited and worth more time. **Zanskar** is a world apart, reached by a long road from Kargil over Pensi La. The **lower Indus** has apricot villages and Brokpa culture. **Changthang** has the lakes, the nomads and the sky.

Some rules matter. Visitors need **inner line permits** for border areas such as Nubra, Pangong, Tso Moriri and Hanle, issued online. Altitude sickness is real: rest for two days, drink water, and go down if symptoms worsen.

spotlights.name: Hanle and the dark sky
spotlights.spot_it: White telescope domes on a bare hill at 4,500 m, under a night sky so clear that the Milky Way casts a glow on the ground.
spotlights.story_md: At about **4,500 m**, with dry air and almost no light pollution, **Hanle** is one of the best astronomy sites in Asia. The **Indian Astronomical Observatory** got first light on its **2-metre Himalayan Chandra Telescope** in **2000**, operated remotely from Bengaluru by satellite link. It also hosts **MACE**, a 21-metre gamma-ray telescope. In **2022** India declared about **1,073 km²** around it the country's **first dark sky reserve**. Local people, many of them women, are trained as **astro-ambassadors** and run telescopes for visitors, earning from the sky rather than the land.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's window on the deep universe.
spotlights.memory_hook: The village that earns from the darkness.

spotlights.name: Drass
spotlights.spot_it: A green valley town of wooden houses under snowy peaks, with the war memorial and Tololing ridge nearby.
spotlights.story_md: **Drass**, at about **3,300 m**, is called the gateway to Ladakh: the first town after **Zoji La** on the road from Srinagar. It is often said to be the second coldest inhabited place in the world; that is a myth, but its winters are fierce, with a recorded low of about **minus 45°C**. Most of its people speak **Shina**. During the **Kargil War** in 1999, the peaks above it, **Tololing** and **Tiger Hill**, were the main battlefields, and the **Kargil War Memorial** stands about 7 km away. Every 26 July it fills with families of the dead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the frontline town of 1999 and Ladakh's western door.
spotlights.memory_hook: The coldest town on the Srinagar road.

spotlights.name: Turtuk

where.label: Turtuk, on the Shyok near the Line of Control

spotlights.when: Indian since December 1971; open to visitors since 2010
spotlights.spot_it: A stone-walled Balti village in apricot orchards on a terrace above the Shyok river, with mountains of Pakistan-held Baltistan ahead.
spotlights.story_md: **Turtuk** was part of Pakistan from 1948 until **December 1971**, when Indian troops led by Major Chewang Rinchen took it overnight. Villagers went to sleep in one country and woke in another, and some families were split for good, with relatives a few kilometres away across the line. Its **3,371** people (2011) are **Balti** Muslims who speak a Tibetic language. It opened to tourists in **2010**, and visitors come for apricots, homestays and the small museum in the house of the old **Yabgo** rulers of Chalunka. It is the last village before the line.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a village that changed countries overnight.
spotlights.memory_hook: Went to bed in Pakistan, woke up in India.

spotlights.name: Phuktal
spotlights.spot_it: A honeycomb of white monastic cells stacked down a sheer cliff around the mouth of a huge cave, above a river gorge.
spotlights.story_md: **Phuktal** grows out of a cave in a cliff in the remote **Lungnak** valley of Zanskar, like a wasp's nest of white cells. Founded in the early 15th century, it belongs to the Gelug school, and for most of its history it could only be reached on foot. Inside the cave is a spring said to have appeared miraculously. In the **1820s** the Hungarian scholar **Alexander Csoma de Kőrös** lived here while studying Tibetan; his work led to the first **Tibetan-English dictionary** (1834). A road now reaches closer, but the last stretch is still a walk.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the most dramatic monasteries in the Himalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: A monastery growing out of a cliff cave.

sections.title: How Ladakh earns
sections.intro_md:
For most of its history Ladakh lived on **subsistence farming, herding and trade**.

Three things then remade the economy. The **army**, which built the roads and became the biggest employer and customer. **Government jobs and subsidies**, which now make up a large share of income. And **tourism**, which started when Ladakh opened to foreigners in **1974**. That first year **527** tourists came. By **2022 and 2023**, arrivals passed **500,000** a year, mostly Indians, boosted by films, social media and motorbike culture.

The next bet is **energy**. Ladakh's high sun and wind make it one of India's best solar sites, and the government has planned a giant renewable park in the Pang area of Changthang, with a long transmission line to the plains. Ladakhis have welcomed the idea of power but worry about grazing land being taken for panels.

spotlights.name: The tourism boom
spotlights.spot_it: Convoys of motorbikes and rented jeeps on high passes, and rows of tents and cafes on the shore of Pangong.
spotlights.story_md: When Ladakh opened to foreigners in **1974**, it drew trekkers and Buddhist seekers. The big change came after **3 Idiots** (2009), when Pangong became a pilgrimage for Indian tourists, and riding a **Royal Enfield** over Khardung La became a rite of passage. Arrivals topped **500,000** in **2022** and in **2023**, in a region of about 300,000 people. Leh now has hundreds of hotels and guesthouses. Water use per tourist is several times a local's, and borewells are falling. Some villages now limit new hotels and push homestays instead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tourism is Ladakh's biggest private earner and biggest strain.
spotlights.memory_hook: More tourists than residents, every year.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
When Ladakh became a union territory in **2019**, many Buddhists in Leh celebrated; they had demanded separation from Kashmir for decades. Within two years the mood had changed across both districts. A UT **without a legislature** meant Ladakh had less say over land and jobs than before. Leh's **Apex Body** and Kargil's **Kargil Democratic Alliance**, rivals for years, joined to demand **statehood**, **Sixth Schedule** protection for tribal land and culture (most Ladakhis are classed as Scheduled Tribes), a second Lok Sabha seat and a public service commission.

Talks with the Home Ministry produced some results. In **June 2025** new rules reserved **85%** of government jobs for local residents, set domicile conditions, reserved one-third of Hill Council seats for women, and made Bhoti and Purgi official languages. But the core demands remained unmet.

Then came the events below. The Lieutenant Governor changed twice: **Kavinder Gupta** from July 2025, then **Vinai Kumar Saxena** from **13 March 2026**. In **April 2026** five new districts were notified, Zanskar, Drass, Sham, Nubra and Changthang, taking the total to seven; Kargil leaders said the new map diluted Muslim-majority areas.

spotlights.name: The Leh protests of September 2025
spotlights.spot_it: A small, quiet capital suddenly under curfew, with burned vehicles outside party offices and soldiers on its main street.
spotlights.story_md: In September 2025, Sonam Wangchuk and others were on a hunger strike in Leh for statehood and the Sixth Schedule. On **24 September**, after two elderly hunger strikers were taken to hospital, a youth-led crowd turned violent: the **BJP office** and Hill Council premises were attacked and vehicles burned. Police opened fire and **four people were killed** and dozens injured. Curfew and an internet shutdown followed. On **26 September** Wangchuk was detained under the **National Security Act** and taken to Jodhpur jail. His wife challenged it in the Supreme Court; the government revoked the detention and he was freed on **14 March 2026**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the worst violence Leh had seen in decades.
spotlights.memory_hook: A peaceful fast, a burned office, four dead.

spotlights.name: The Zoji La tunnel

where.label: Zoji La, between Sonamarg and Drass

spotlights.spot_it: Today: a narrow dirt road cut into cliffs with walls of snow and lines of trucks. Soon: a tunnel portal at about 3,000 m.
spotlights.story_md: **Zoji La**, at about **3,528 m**, is the lowest pass into Ladakh but one of the deadliest, closed by snow and avalanches for roughly **five to six months** a year. A **13.15 km** tunnel beneath it, one of the longest road tunnels in Asia, was begun in earnest in **2020**. A June **2026** update reported the breakthrough achieved and the work about **85%** complete, with opening targeted for **February 2028**. Together with a tunnel at Z-Morh, it will give Ladakh its first year-round road to Kashmir, cutting the crossing to minutes and changing winter life for Kargil and Drass.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It will end Ladakh's winter isolation by road.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three hours over the pass, fifteen minutes under it.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Ladakh attracts legends.

The common ones: **'Jesus studied in Ladakh.'** A hoax, examined below. **'Magnetic Hill pulls cars uphill.'** An optical illusion. **'Khardung La is the highest road in the world.'** Its sign overstates its height by about 240 m. **'Drass is the second coldest inhabited place on Earth.'** Very cold, but towns in Siberia are far colder. **'The Brokpa are the last pure Aryans.'** There is no pure race, and no evidence for the claims built on it. **'Ladakh is Little Tibet.'** It shares Tibet's religion and roots, but has been a separate kingdom for most of a thousand years, and nearly half its people are Muslim.

spotlights.name: The 'Jesus in Hemis' hoax
spotlights.spot_it: A 19th-century book cover in French promising 'the unknown life of Jesus Christ', and a monastery that denies the story.
spotlights.story_md: In **1894** a Russian adventurer, **Nicolas Notovitch**, published a book claiming that at **Hemis**, while recovering from a broken leg, he had been shown a Tibetan manuscript, the **Life of Saint Issa**, describing Jesus studying in India in his 'lost years'. The scholar **Max Müller** wrote to the monastery, whose head lama replied that no Westerner had visited in fifteen years and no such text existed. In **1895** a professor from Agra, **J. Archibald Douglas**, went to Hemis and got the same denial. Notovitch is later said to have admitted inventing it. No scholar today accepts the story, yet it still sells books and tours.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a textbook case of a fabricated source.
spotlights.memory_hook: No visitor, no manuscript, no Jesus.

spotlights.name: Magnetic Hill

where.label: Leh to Kargil highway near Nimmu

spotlights.spot_it: A yellow signboard on a straight stretch of road with a painted box where drivers stop their car in neutral.
spotlights.story_md: About 30 km from Leh on the Kargil road, a signboard tells drivers to park in a marked box, put the car in neutral and watch it roll 'uphill'. Some versions add that aircraft avoid the area because of magnetism. The truth is an **optical illusion**: the surrounding slopes hide the horizon, so a slight **downhill** road looks like it climbs. The same effect exists at dozens of 'gravity hills' around the world. If the hill were really magnetic, it would pull on steel, not on aluminium cans and water, which also 'roll uphill' there.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a lesson in how easily the eye is fooled without a horizon.
spotlights.memory_hook: The road goes down; your brain says up.

sections.title: Recap: Ladakh in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. Ladakh is India's **largest and emptiest union territory**: about 59,000 km² and 274,000 people in 2011.
2. It is a **cold desert** in the Himalayan rain shadow: about 100 mm of rain, all water from snow and ice.
3. Its people are about **46% Muslim** (mostly Shia, in Kargil) and **40% Buddhist** (mostly in Leh).
4. It was an independent **Namgyal kingdom** from 1460 to 1834, when the Dogras of Jammu took it.
5. **Alchi** preserves the Buddhist painting of medieval Kashmir.
6. It borders both **China and Pakistan**: Siachen (1984), Kargil (1999) and Galwan (2020) are its flashpoints.
7. About **477 of India's 718 snow leopards** live here.
8. The **perak**, **pashmina**, **butter tea** and **masked cham dances** are its signature culture.
9. Tourism grew from **527 visitors in 1974 to over 500,000** a year.
10. Since 2019 it has been a **UT without a legislature**; the fight for statehood and the Sixth Schedule led to deadly protests in September 2025 and Sonam Wangchuk's jailing until March 2026.

verification.claim: Ladakh's area
verification.note: The area India administers is usually given as about 59,146 km²; India's official claim, including Aksai Chin and Gilgit-Baltistan, is far larger. Some tables sum to 66,000 km² or more.

verification.claim: Number of districts in 2026
verification.note: Five new districts were notified in April 2026, giving seven; one Wikipedia list names eight including Sankoo. We use seven.

verification.claim: Founding date of Hemis monastery
verification.note: Sources give the 1630s, 1672 or an earlier foundation refounded in the 17th century.

verification.claim: Date of the Mulbekh Maitreya
verification.note: Most scholars say 7th to 8th century; local tradition says Kushan era, 1st to 3rd century.

verification.claim: Alchi founded by Rinchen Zangpo
verification.note: Tradition credits him; inscriptions point to local patrons in the 12th to 13th century.

verification.claim: Number of Chewang Norphel's artificial glaciers
verification.note: Accounts give 12 to 15.

verification.claim: Chinese deaths at Galwan
verification.note: China says 4; Indian and independent estimates range from about 35 to 45.

verification.claim: Umling La is the world's highest motorable road at 5,798 m
verification.note: Recognised by Guinness in 2021 on BRO figures; independent elevation data and rival roads in Tibet and Bolivia are debated.

verification.claim: Number of Bactrian camels in Nubra
verification.note: Estimates range from about 200 to about 400.

verification.claim: The Brokpa are 'pure Aryans' visited by foreign women seeking children
verification.note: Repeated in sensational media since the 1990s; no scientific or documented basis.

verification.claim: Losar moved earlier because of a 17th-century king's war
verification.note: The standard local explanation; the king and date vary between tellings.

verification.claim: Snow leopard and black-necked crane adopted as UT animal and bird in 2021
verification.note: Widely reported in 2021; we did not see the original notification.

verification.claim: Size of the planned Pang renewable park
verification.note: Usually given as about 13 GW with battery storage; plans and sites have changed since 2023.

verification.claim: Tourist arrivals above 500,000 in 2022 and 2023
verification.note: Figures vary by source and by whether day visitors and pilgrims are counted.

verification.claim: Mughal condition that the Ladakhi king convert to Islam
verification.note: Kashmiri accounts say the king converted; Ladakhi chronicles do not mention it.

best_facts.fact: An engineer froze a stream into a 6-metre cone of ice in 2013 to irrigate fields in spring, using no pump at all: gravity pushes the water up the pipe.
best_facts.why_surprising: A glacier you can build in a weekend.

best_facts.fact: Turtuk's villagers went to sleep in Pakistan and woke in India in December 1971, and some families have been split by the line ever since.
best_facts.why_surprising: A village that changed countries overnight.

best_facts.fact: At Galwan in 2020, twenty Indian soldiers died in a fight with Chinese troops in which no guns were used, only stones, batons and clubs.
best_facts.why_surprising: A deadly modern battle fought like a medieval brawl.

best_facts.fact: The man who inspired Phunsukh Wangdu in 3 Idiots spent nearly six months in jail under the National Security Act after the 2025 Leh protests.
Leh gets about 100 mm of rain a year, desert levels, yet Ladakh grows barley, apricots and willows entirely on meltwater.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Himalayan valley drier than parts of the Sahara.

best_facts.fact: Khardung La's famous sign claims 5,602 m, but satellite and GPS data put the pass at about 5,359 m.
best_facts.why_surprising: A world-famous number off by about 240 metres.

best_facts.fact: Roughly two-thirds of India's snow leopards, about 477 of 718, live in Ladakh.
best_facts.why_surprising: One region holds most of a country's big cats of the snow.

best_facts.fact: Leh Palace, nine storeys of mud and stone, was built around 1600, decades before Lhasa's Potala, which it is usually said to copy.
In 1894 a Russian claimed Hemis held a manuscript proving Jesus studied in India; the head lama said no Westerner had visited in fifteen years.
best_facts.why_surprising: A famous 'lost gospel' that never existed.

best_facts.fact: Ladakh is about 46% Muslim and 40% Buddhist, so it is not the purely Buddhist 'Little Tibet' of travel brochures.
best_facts.why_surprising: The brochure image misses half the people.

best_facts.fact: India's only Bactrian camels, in Nubra, descend from Silk Road caravan animals stranded when the trade route to Yarkand closed around 1950.
best_facts.why_surprising: Two-humped camels are a leftover of the Silk Road.

best_facts.fact: In 1974 Ladakh had 527 tourists; by 2022 and 2023 it had more than 500,000 a year, almost twice its population.
best_facts.why_surprising: A thousandfold rise in fifty years.

best_facts.fact: Ladakhi Buddhists celebrate their new year about two months before Tibetans do, a change traditionally traced to a king going to war.
best_facts.why_surprising: A calendar moved for a battle.

best_facts.fact: Hanle has India's first dark sky reserve, where local women trained as astro-ambassadors run telescopes for tourists.
Chewang Rinchen won the Maha Vir Chakra at about 17 in 1948, and a second one in 1971 for taking Turtuk.
best_facts.why_surprising: A teenage war hero who won again 23 years later.

best_facts.fact: Alchi's temples stopped being used for worship around the 15th century, which helped preserve the best surviving Kashmiri Buddhist murals anywhere.
A traditional Ladakhi compost toilet uses no water at all and turns waste into field fertiliser within about a year.
best_facts.why_surprising: Old sanitation that solves a modern water crisis.

best_facts.fact: Ice hockey, not cricket, is Ladakh's most popular sport, played on natural ice from mid-December to mid-February.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's cricket rule stops at the Zoji La.

side_dish.title: What thin air does to your body
side_dish.body_md:
At Leh's 3,500 m, the air still has 21% oxygen, the same share as at sea level. What changes is pressure. There is about a third less air above you pushing down, so each breath carries about a third fewer oxygen molecules into your lungs.

The body notices within minutes. You breathe faster and your heart beats faster to move more blood. Over a day or two the kidneys make the blood slightly more acidic so you can keep breathing hard, which is why some people feel tingling fingers. Over weeks, the body makes more red blood cells to carry oxygen.

If you climb faster than the body can adjust, you can get **acute mountain sickness**: headache, nausea, poor sleep, tiredness. Rarer but dangerous are fluid in the lungs (HAPE) and swelling of the brain (HACE). The cure for all three is the same: **go down**.

That is why Leh's hotels tell flying visitors to rest for 48 hours, and why the rule for trekkers is to climb slowly and sleep low. Ladakhis and Tibetans have lived at this height for generations. Tibetans carry a version of a gene called **EPAS1** that helps them avoid making too many red blood cells, which would thicken the blood. Studies have found this gene variant came from the **Denisovans**, an extinct human group, passed on through ancient interbreeding. Some of that inheritance may be in the people who greet you with Julley.

offline_task.title: Make a pot of skyu, Ladakh's thumb-pressed pasta stew
offline_task.body_md:
**Skyu for two:** mix 1 cup of whole-wheat flour with a pinch of salt and enough water to make a firm dough. Rest it 15 minutes. Roll it into a thin rope, pinch off pea-sized pieces, and press each one with your thumb against your palm to make a small cup.

In a pot, warm a tablespoon of butter or oil and fry a chopped onion and a crushed garlic clove until soft. Add one diced potato, one diced turnip or carrot, a handful of peas or spinach, and about 4 cups of water or stock. Simmer for 10 minutes, then drop in the dough cups and cook for another 10 to 12 minutes until they are tender and the broth has thickened. Season with salt, a pinch of turmeric if you like, and finish with a spoon of butter. Some families add milk at the end for a creamy version.

While it cooks, notice how few ingredients there are. This is food built for a place where little grows and fuel is precious: one pot, slow heat, filling for a cold night. If you want the full experience, drink a cup of salted tea with butter alongside it.
